advances: Refutes the proposed scalar implication from an exact midpoint log-concavity defect \(\kappa\) to an absolute lower bound \(c\kappa\) for both masses at the true mean, even when \(\kappa\) is restricted to inverse powers of two. The counterfamily is compactly supported, bounded, and positive throughout the interior, and satisfies the midpoint condition for every pair of points. This obstructs that scalar bridge; it does not refute the locked mixed-integer target or any higher-dimensional lattice midpoint-count statement.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The construction and all midpoint, integrability, mean, and mass checks are proved above.
proof:
Fix an integer \(N\ge16\), and put \(D=2^N\), \(\kappa=\kappa_N=\sqrt N/D\), \(\lambda=(\log D)/D\), and \(h(x)=e^{-\lambda x}=D^{-x/D}\). These definitions are local to this scalar counterfamily. In particular, \(0<\kappa<1\).

Let \(\mathcal D\) be the dyadic rational numbers in \([0,1]\). Define a function \(r\) on \(\mathcal D\) as follows. Set \(r(0)=r(1)=0\). If \(t\in\mathcal D\setminus\{0,1\}\) has its lowest-term form \(t=j/2^m\), where \(m\ge1\) and \(j\) is odd, set \(r(t)=2-2^{1-m}\).

This function satisfies \(r((s+t)/2)\le1+(r(s)+r(t))/2\) for all \(s,t\in\mathcal D\). To check this exactly, if both arguments are endpoints, their midpoint is an endpoint or \(1/2\), with value respectively \(0\) or \(1\). If just one argument is an endpoint and the other has denominator level \(m\ge1\), the midpoint has denominator level at most \(m+1\). Its value is therefore at most \(2-2^{-m}=1+(2-2^{1-m})/2\). If both arguments are interior dyadics, each value is at least \(1\), so the right-hand side is at least \(2\), whereas every value of \(r\) is less than \(2\).

For \(x\in[0,D+1]\), define
\[
g_D(x)=\min\{r(t):t\in\mathcal D,\ 0\le x-Dt\le1\},
\qquad
f_N(x)=h(x)\kappa^{g_D(x)}.
\]
Set \(f_N(x)=0\) outside this interval. The minimum exists: the intervals \([j,j+1]\), \(0\le j\le D\), cover \([0,D+1]\), and their parameters \(t=j/D\) are dyadics of denominator level at most \(N\). Because the values \(2-2^{1-m}\) increase with \(m\), a minimizing parameter has level at most \(N\). Hence \(g_D\) has only finitely many values, and its sublevel sets are finite unions of closed intervals. Thus \(f_N\) is measurable, bounded by \(1\), integrable, and strictly positive on \([0,D+1]\). On both intervals \([0,1]\) and \([D,D+1]\), it equals \(h\).

To verify the full midpoint condition, take \(x,y\in[0,D+1]\) and minimizing parameters \(t,s\in\mathcal D\). Write \(x=Dt+u\) and \(y=Ds+v\), with \(u,v\in[0,1]\). Their midpoint belongs to \([D(t+s)/2,D(t+s)/2+1]\). The proved inequality for \(r\) gives
\[
g_D((x+y)/2)
\le r((t+s)/2)
\le1+\frac{g_D(x)+g_D(y)}2.
\]
Since \(\kappa<1\) and \(h((x+y)/2)=\sqrt{h(x)h(y)}\), this implies \(f_N((x+y)/2)\ge\kappa\sqrt{f_N(x)f_N(y)}\). If either argument lies outside the support, the right-hand side is zero and the same inequality holds. Thus it holds for every real pair, including support boundaries.

We next bound the total mass outside the left interval. Write \(R=\int_1^{D+1}f_N(x)\,dx\). The right interval has mass at most \(1/D\). Every other point, apart from irrelevant interval endpoints, has a minimizing parameter with some level \(m\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), of the form \(j/2^m\) with \(j\) odd and \(1\le j<2^m\). Its density is then \(h(x)\kappa^{2-2^{1-m}}\), on the interval \([Dj/2^m,Dj/2^m+1]\). Consequently, by an upper bound over all these intervals,
\[
R\le \frac1D+
\sum_{m=1}^N\kappa^{2-2^{1-m}}
\sum_{\substack{1\le j<2^m\\j\text{ odd}}}
\int_{Dj/2^m}^{Dj/2^m+1}h(x)\,dx.
\]
For a fixed \(m\), put \(a_m=(\log D)/2^m\). Since \(h\) decreases, the inner sum is at most the infinite geometric sum \(e^{-a_m}/(1-e^{-2a_m})\). Also \(-\log\kappa=\log D-(\log N)/2\). Thus the summand corresponding to \(m\) is at most
\[
\kappa^2
\frac{\exp((\log D-\log N)/2^m)}{1-e^{-2a_m}}
\le \kappa^2\frac{e^{a_m}}{1-e^{-2a_m}}.
\]
If \(a_m\ge1\), then \(1-e^{-2a_m}\ge1/2\) and \(e^{a_m}\le e^{(\log D)/2}=\sqrt D\). These indices contribute at most \(2N\sqrt D\) to the sum of the displayed fractions. For \(N\ge16\), the elementary inequality \(N^2\le2^{N/2}=\sqrt D\) gives \(2N\sqrt D\le2D/N\). One proof of this elementary inequality is induction: equality holds at \(N=16\), and \(((N+1)/N)^2\le(17/16)^2<\sqrt2\) preserves it.

If \(0<a_m<1\), then \(e^{a_m}<3\) and \(1-e^{-2a_m}\ge a_m/2\). For the latter bound, \(e^{2a_m}\ge1+2a_m\) gives \(1-e^{-2a_m}\ge2a_m/(1+2a_m)\ge2a_m/3\). Therefore these indices contribute at most
\[
\sum_{m=1}^N\frac{6\,2^m}{\log D}
\le\frac{12D}{\log D}
\le\frac{24D}{N},
\]
where \(\log2\ge1/2\) was used in the last step. Combining the two ranges and using \(\kappa^2=N/D^2\) proves \(R\le1/D+\kappa^2(26D/N)=27/D\). All these are analytic bounds on the explicitly defined density, with no numerical feasibility assertion.

Let \(F=\int_{\mathbb R}f_N(x)\,dx\) and \(\mu_N=F^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}xf_N(x)\,dx\). Since \(\lambda=N\log2/2^N\le1/16\) for \(N\ge16\), we have \(e^{-\lambda}\ge1-\lambda\ge15/16\). The mass bounds give
\[
\frac{15}{16}\le\int_0^1h(x)\,dx\le F\le1+\frac{27}{D}.
\]
The first moments of the two endpoint intervals alone give
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}xf_N(x)\,dx
\ge\int_0^1xh(x)\,dx+\int_D^{D+1}xh(x)\,dx
\ge\frac{e^{-\lambda}}2+e^{-\lambda}
\ge\frac{45}{32}.
\]
In the right interval we used \(x\ge D\) and \(h(x)\ge D^{-1}e^{-\lambda}\). Because \(D\ge2^{16}\), \(1+27/D<45/32\). Thus the true mean satisfies \(\mu_N>1\). It follows that
\[
\frac{\int_{\mu_N}^{\infty}f_N(x)\,dx}{F}
\le\frac{R}{F}
\le\frac{27}{D}\frac{16}{15}
<\frac{30}{D}.
\]
The ratio of this cap mass to \(\kappa_N\) is at most \(30/\sqrt N\), which tends to zero. For any proposed \(c>0\), choose an integer \(N\ge16\) with \(30/\sqrt N<c\); then this function violates the claimed right-half-line lower bound. The choice \(N=4^k\) gives \(\sqrt N=2^k\), hence \(\kappa_N=2^{-(4^k-k)}\) and the same ratio bound becomes \(30/2^k\), still tending to zero. This disproves the simultaneous bound for both half-lines even under the inverse-power-of-two restriction. Reflection of the counterfamily also gives the analogous failure on the left.
statement:
There is no absolute constant \(c>0\) with the following property: whenever \(0<\kappa\le1\) and a bounded integrable function \(f:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) is supported on a compact interval, is positive in its interior, and satisfies \(f((x+y)/2)\ge\kappa\sqrt{f(x)f(y)}\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), both closed half-lines at its normalized mean have normalized mass at least \(c\kappa\).

More precisely, for every integer \(N\ge16\) there is such a function \(f_N\), with \(\kappa_N=\sqrt N/2^N\) and mean \(\mu_N\), for which
\[
\frac{\int_{\mu_N}^{\infty} f_N(x)\,dx}{\int_{\mathbb R} f_N(x)\,dx}
\le \frac{30}{2^N}
=\frac{30}{\sqrt N}\,\kappa_N.
\]
Along \(N=4^k\), with integer \(k\ge2\), the defect is exactly \(\kappa_N=2^{-(4^k-k)}\), so the same failure occurs for inverse powers of two.
